title: Space-efficient lists
lead: An Advanced section on lists that waste little space: ODS’s RootishArrayStack, the √n lower bound on wasted space, and the SEList; computing square roots in constant time is Beyond. Blocks and list indices count from 0. The SEList proof’s “potential method” is Section 1.5’s method used as a counter: Φ is the number of fragile nodes, each add that does not spread raises it by at most 1, and so the adds before a spread pay for it.
notes: The Discussion and Exercises sections of ODS’s two chapters are left out here.
exercise_notes: No exercise ships with this section yet. ODS’s test_rootisharraystack.py and test_selist.py are tests with no printed statement (they pass on ODS’s Python once its integer division and print statements are ported). ODS Exercises 2.10 to 2.13 (faster RootishArrayStack variants and a CubishArrayStack) and 3.17 and 3.18 (an SEList used as a stack and a variant of it) have no published answers or tests and are left out. No open exercise exists for computing square roots in constant time or for the √n lower bound on wasted space.

assumes.text: The $\mathrm{remove}(i)$ operation ensures that a RootishArrayStack never has more than two blocks that are not completely full.
Block $b$ contains $b + 1$ elements, so blocks $0, \ldots, r - 3$ hold $1 + 2 + \cdots + (r-2) = (r-2)(r-1)/2$ of them.

then.why: All but the last two of the $r$ blocks are full, and their elements are among the $n$.

steps.cap: A parabola that opens upward is at most 0 only between its roots, and by the quadratic formula the larger root of $r^2 - 3r + (2 - 2n)$ is $\frac{1}{2}\left(3 + \sqrt{9 - 4(2 - 2n)}\right)$.

assumes.text: An empty data structure receives $n$ items one at a time, and at the end they are distributed among $r$ memory blocks.
The pigeonhole principle: $n$ items in $r$ blocks put at least $n/r$ of them in one block.
Immediately after it is allocated, a block is empty, so all of its space is wasted.
The structure must keep $r$ pointers (or references) to its $r$ blocks, and these pointers are wasted space.

then.why: The $r$ pointers are wasted at the end, and the large block was wasting its space the moment it was allocated.

steps.cap: If $r \ge \sqrt{n}$, the first is at least $\sqrt{n}$; if $r < \sqrt{n}$, then $n/r > n/\sqrt{n} = \sqrt{n}$.

derivations.source: Open Data Structures, 2.6.4 Computing Square Roots, the proof of Lemma 2.3

then.why: The square root is increasing, and $\sqrt{1} = 1$.

steps.cap: Both sides are squares: $x - \sqrt{x} \ge 0$ because $x \ge \sqrt{x}$ when $x \ge 1$, and $x - 2\sqrt{x} + 1 = (\sqrt{x} - 1)^2$.
Both bases are at least 0, $\sqrt{x} - 1$ by the first line, and for numbers at least 0, $p^2 \ge q^2$ gives $p \ge q$.

then.why: Taking away at most $\sqrt{x}$ leaves at least $x - \sqrt{x}$.

derivations.source: Open Data Structures, 3.3.4 Amortized Analysis of Spreading and Gathering, the proof of Lemma 3.1

assumes.text: The potential $\Phi$, the number of fragile nodes, starts at 0 and is never less than 0.
Each time Case 1 or Case 2 occurs, the potential increases by at most 1.
Each time Case 3 occurs, the potential decreases by $b - 1$.
Of the $m$ calls to $\mathrm{add}(i,x)$, $s$ reach Case 3 and call $\mathrm{spread}(u)$, and the other $m - s$ are Case 1 or Case 2.

then.why: The potential starts at 0, the $m - s$ other calls add at most 1 each, and each spread takes $b - 1$ away.

assumes.text: Each call to $\mathrm{spread}(u)$ runs two nested loops of at most $b + 1$ steps, so it takes $O(b^2)$ time.
